query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying controlled in‐situ substrate preheating during additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will reduce the thermal gradients during solidification, thereby lowering residual stresses, minimizing element segregation and defect formation, and ultimately improving the mechanical integrity of the fabricated parts relative to those made with an unheated substrate.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi fabricated by standard additive manufacturing processes (such as L-PBF or DED) at ambient substrate temperature, where rapid cooling creates high thermal gradients that lead to segregation, residual stresses, and process‐induced defects.
generation.intervention: Maintain the build substrate at a moderate elevated temperature (e.g., in the 200–400 °C range) in situ during the additive manufacturing process.
generation.conditions: Applicable to additive manufacturing processes for high-entropy alloys such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) or direct energy deposition (DED) with process parameters similar to those optimized for AlCrFeNiSi powders; mechanical testing performed at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in thermal gradients leads to a slower, more uniform solidification rate that refines the grain structure, decreases dislocation buildup and chemical segregation, and minimizes the formation of voids or cracks.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the substrate decreases the temperature difference between the melt pool and the build platform, thereby reducing the cooling rate. This diminishes the driving force for rapid solidification, limits non-equilibrium segregation of alloying elements, and reduces the nucleation of residual stresses and defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples produced with substrate preheating will exhibit lower residual stress levels, more uniform elemental distribution (as revealed by finer, less segregated microstructures in EDS/SEM analyses) and improved mechanical performance—such as higher ductility and a more favorable yield strength-to-strength ratio—compared to conventionally fabricated parts.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed AlCrFeNiSi parts produced with ambient substrate temperature, which typically show pronounced compositional segregation, elevated residual stresses, and higher defect density.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected to be significant when using AM methods (LPBF or DED) under similar energy input regimes that do not inherently induce excessive grain growth; however, if preheating is too high or applied to geometries with drastically different cooling conditions, grain coarsening or other unintended microstructural changes might occur.
generation.uncertainty: While multiple studies on similar HEA systems (e.g., the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA in PMC12113129 and in situ heat treatment effects in H13 tool steel in PMC12654052) support the advantage of thermal management in reducing residual stresses and segregation, the optimal preheating temperature and its specific effects on the AlCrFeNiSi system remain uncertain. The extrapolation from analogous alloys and processing regimes (as evidenced in PMC12113129 and PMC10971808) forms the basis of the proposal, but the unique behavior of this cobalt-free system has not been directly established.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using an identical AM process except that one set employs a controlled in-situ substrate preheating (e.g., at 300 °C) and the other uses a standard ambient temperature substrate. After fabrication, perform detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM/EDS, EBSD, and XRD for residual stress analysis) and mechanical testing (tensile tests, hardness measurements).
measurements: Residual stress levels (via XRD or hole-drilling methods)
Chemical homogeneity and grain structure (via SEM/EDS and EBSD)
Mechanical properties such as yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
Defect density and crack incidence (microscopy evaluations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with substrate preheating do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stresses, reduced segregation and defects, and do not achieve improved mechanical properties compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) have emerged as a focus in high-performance materials research due to their exceptional mechanical properties and high-temperature stability [,,]. In recent years, researchers have fabricated EHEAs through various manufacturing processes, such as casting, selective laser melting (SLM), and direct energy deposition (DED), and they further investigated the regulatory effects of heat treatment on their microstructure and mechanical properties. By synthesizing recent research advances, this review specifically addresses the critical role of heat treatment in optimizing the performance of EHEAs. Heat treatment has been demonstrated to facilitate the microstructural optimization of as-casting AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs [,,]. Researchers, including Sudeep Kumar T. et al., have found that homogenization annealing effectively reduces compositional segregation in the as-casting microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi2, thereby enhancing the alloy’s uniformity []. In dual-phase EHEAs, heat treatment can regulate phase proportions and phase boundary structures, leading to improved mechanical properties [].
